Ink-wash Feng originates from traditional Chinese ink wash painting. In the Tang Dynasty, Wu Daozi and Wang Wei established the systematic techniques of ink wash art, marking the formal formation of the ink-wash style.
During the Republic of China era (1912–1949), Chinese art underwent a period of rapid modernization and cultural experimentation. The
became one of the most influential movements of the period, combining classical ink painting with Western realism, perspective, and contemporary subject matter. At the same time, artists such as

promoted the integration of European academic techniques into Chinese art. The resulting fusion of expressive ink painting and modern artistic ideas laid much of the foundation for the aesthetics later associated with Shuimo Feng.

After the founding of the People’s Republic of China in 1949, state-sponsored art programs encouraged innovation that honored cultural heritage while embracing modern media. In the 1960s and 80s, pioneering animators at the Shanghai Animation Film Studio began adapting classical ink wash aesthetics into short films, emphasizing fluid brushwork, and atmospheric landscapes. These works became some of the most celebrated achievements of Chinese animation and are widely regarded in China as cultural classics.

The continued popularity of ink-wash-inspired aesthetics in modern Chinese media can be traced in part to the lasting cultural impact and nostalgic appeal of these landmark animated films, which helped introduce traditional brush-and-ink imagery to generations of viewers in a modern context. With digital development in modern times, it further crossed boundaries, expanding to films, graphic design, fashion, cultural creation and all modern design fields worldwide.
